newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-SOUTH AFRICA BLOCK OVERSEAS MOVES.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-SOUTH AFRICA BLOCK OVERSEAS MOVES.

text.p: The exodus of South African World Cup stars to England and other overseas rugby nations has been blocked by the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU).

"International Rugby Board (IRFB) regulation number nine says that any player that wants to play outside his country has to be (first) released by his union. We will not be doing that from now on," Rian Oberholzer, chief executive of SARFU, told Reuters in Cape Town on Tuesday.

"We are losing a stream of players and we cannot permit it to go on. We have a responsibility to keep provincial and club rugby in South Africa strong. We cannot allow our domestic game to become devalued."
Officials from the IRFB in Dublin confirmed that South Africa had the power to prevent its players from signing lucrative overseas contracts.

"It is a domestic matter between South Africa and its players," said IRFB spokesman Peter McMullan. "The South Africa union is saying that it wants South Africa players to remain in the country and be involved in the South African game. The regulation is very clear that the individual unions have that power."

World Cup winning captain Francois Pienaar (Saracens) and Joel Stransky (Leicester), the flyhalf who clinched the World Cup final against New Zealand with an extra-time drop goal, caused front page sensations in South Africa when they switched to English club rugby this season.

But they are part of a steady haemorrhaging of South African talent. Other Springboks to have been lured to England -- where the pound's strength against the rand is an undeniable attraction -- include lock Steve Atherton (Bath), back-rower Rudolf Streuli (Bedford), and hooker John Allan (London Scottish). Transvaal utility back Lance Sherrell has also joined Milan in Italy.
"We cannot allow professionalism to steal our lifeblood," said Oberholzer.
Other Springboks are continually rumoured to be on the brink of moves to wealthy English clubs.
Oberholzer added: "Another thing we are considering is to follow the example of New Zealand. They do not pick players for the All Blacks who do not play in New Zealand.
"We could say, 'if you want to play for South Africa you have to be in this country'."
Oberholzer said he did not expect his union's authority to be challenged in the law courts.

"That will be a matter for the legal experts, for the civil courts," the IRFB's McMullan said, adding that any player currently in South Africa who ignored the ruling could be banned by the local union from representing South Africa.
"But again, what sanctions they would impose on someone defying the ruling...is a domestic matter."
Part of IRFB regulation nine states: "Subject to any legal requirements in the country of its jurisdiction, a Union may pass regulations further restricting player movement."
The season kicks off in South Africa on March 1 with the Super 12 series and ends for the country's internationals on December 6 with an international against Scotland at Murrayfield.
